cards.title: The Four-Questions Framework
cards.teaser: Adam Shostack's four questions from Threat Modeling: Designing for Security turn an open-ended creative exercise into a structured engineering practice. Ask them in order on every design, every major change, and after every incident.

runs.text: In
Threat Modeling: Designing for Security

(2014), Adam Shostack argues that all threat modeling, regardless of methodology, can be reduced to four questions. They work at any level of formality — on a whiteboard in a 30-minute sprint or in a week-long structured analysis.

items.text: What are we building?
Understand the system through diagrams, data flows, and trust boundaries. You cannot identify threats against a system you have not modeled.
What could go wrong?
Enumerate threats using a structured method such as STRIDE. Brainstorm attacker goals, abuse cases, and misuse scenarios.
What are we going to do about it?
For each threat, decide: mitigate, accept, transfer, or avoid. Assign owners and track items in the backlog.
Did we do a good job?
Retrospect on the process quality: Was the model complete? Were assumptions validated? Did discovered threats make it into the sprint?

runs.text: Shostack's insight is that most teams fail threat modeling not because they use the wrong methodology but because they skip question 1 (they never draw a diagram) or question 4 (they never check whether their mitigations actually shipped). The four questions are a checklist against those omissions.
Shostack led the development of Microsoft's SDL threat modeling practice and co-authored the CVE and CVSS frameworks. His book is the canonical practitioner reference for the field.
Threat modeling is four questions asked in order: draw your system, list what could go wrong, decide what to do about each problem, then check whether you actually did it.

cards.title: Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs)
cards.teaser: A Data Flow Diagram is the primary artifact of threat modeling — it makes trust boundaries and data movement legible. A DFD drawn before an architecture discussion is worth more than ten hours of post-deployment security review.

runs.text: DFDs originated in structured systems analysis (DeMarco, 1979) but were adopted by security practitioners because they expose exactly the information threat modeling needs: where data originates, where it travels, where it is stored, and where it crosses privilege or trust levels.
A DFD uses four element types:

items.text: External entities
(rectangles) — actors outside the system boundary: browsers, mobile apps, third-party APIs, humans.
Processes
(circles/rounded boxes) — code that transforms data: web servers, microservices, lambda functions.
Data stores
(parallel lines) — places data rests: databases, caches, file systems, queues.
Data flows
(arrows) — movement of data between elements, labeled with the data type and protocol.

runs.text: A minimal ASCII DFD for a login flow:

explanation.code:
[Browser] ---(HTTPS POST /login)---> [Auth Service] ---(SQL query)---> [=Users DB=]
    |                                       |
    |<--(JWT, Set-Cookie: session)----------|
    |                                       |
    +-- trust boundary (Internet) ---------+-- trust boundary (internal network)

Legend:
  [  ]  = External entity
  [  ]  = Process (Auth Service)
  [= =] = Data store
  --->  = Data flow
  ///   = Trust boundary

runs.text: DFDs are typically drawn at two levels of detail: Level 0 (context diagram — the whole system as one process surrounded by its external actors) and Level 1 (individual services and data stores expanded). Most threat modeling sessions work at Level 1.
Every data flow that crosses a trust boundary is a candidate threat surface. If your DFD has no trust boundaries drawn, you have not modeled your system — you have drawn an architecture diagram.
A DFD is a map of your system that shows who owns what and where data has to cross from one owner to another. Those crossing points are where attackers do their work.

cards.title: Trust Boundaries
cards.teaser: A trust boundary is any line a DFD arrow crosses where the receiving side cannot blindly trust the data it receives. Every trust boundary is a mandatory validation point — and every missing validation is a potential vulnerability.

runs.text: Trust boundaries divide a system into zones based on who controls the data and code in each zone. Data moving from a lower-trust zone to a higher-trust zone must be validated; data moving from a higher-trust zone to a lower-trust zone must be sanitized.
Common trust boundaries in web applications:

items.text: Internet / DMZ
— the outermost boundary. All input from the browser or mobile client is untrusted. Validation happens at the application layer, not just the firewall.
DMZ / internal network
— the load balancer or API gateway hands off to internal services. Even here, requests should be authenticated (zero-trust networking assumes no implicit trust).
Service / database
— SQL queries, Redis commands, and message-queue payloads are data flows across this boundary. Parameterized queries enforce the boundary against injection.
User context / admin context
— privilege escalation attacks cross this logical boundary. Authorization checks enforce it.
Process / OS
— shell commands and file-system calls are data flows to the OS. Command injection and path traversal attacks exploit insufficient validation here.

runs.text: The discipline of drawing trust boundaries forces a team to answer: "Who is responsible for validating data at this point?" If nobody can answer, the boundary is unguarded.

Zero-trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) formalizes the idea that trust boundaries exist everywhere — even within what was traditionally called the "internal network." Every service-to-service call must be authenticated and authorized.
A trust boundary is a line that says: data on this side is controlled by a different party than data on that side. Crossing it without checking the data is what most vulnerabilities have in common.

cards.title: STRIDE
cards.teaser: STRIDE is a mnemonic for six threat categories developed at Microsoft in the late 1990s. It turns the open-ended question "what could go wrong?" into a structured checklist that can be applied to every element in a DFD.

runs.text: Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg introduced STRIDE at Microsoft in 1999. Each letter maps to a threat category and to the security property it violates:

items.text: S — Spoofing
(violates Authentication) — impersonating another user, service, or process. Examples: stolen session tokens, forged JWTs, ARP spoofing.
T — Tampering
(violates Integrity) — modifying data in transit or at rest. Examples: MITM HTTP modification, SQL UPDATE by unauthorized user, log file editing.
R — Repudiation
(violates Non-repudiation) — denying having performed an action. Examples: no audit log, deletable logs, unsigned API requests.
I — Information Disclosure
(violates Confidentiality) — exposing data to unauthorized parties. Examples: verbose error messages, insecure direct object reference, unencrypted database backups.
D — Denial of Service
(violates Availability) — making a system unavailable. Examples: resource exhaustion, slowloris attacks, ReDoS (regex denial of service).
E — Elevation of Privilege
(violates Authorization) — gaining permissions not intended. Examples: IDOR, directory traversal, container escape.

runs.text: STRIDE's strength is completeness: the six categories cover the full space of security properties (CIA + AAA). Its weakness is that it identifies threats without ranking them — you need a separate risk-scoring step (DREAD, CVSS, or qualitative triage) to prioritize.

STRIDE maps directly to countermeasures: Spoofing → authentication; Tampering → integrity controls and signing; Repudiation → audit logging; Information Disclosure → encryption and access control; DoS → rate limiting and resource quotas; EoP → least-privilege authorization.
STRIDE is six ways an attacker can hurt you: pretend to be someone else, change data, deny doing something, steal data, crash the system, or grab more permissions than they should have.

cards.title: STRIDE-per-Element
cards.teaser: STRIDE-per-element applies each threat category to each DFD element type. Not all STRIDE categories apply equally to all element types — the matrix guides analysts toward the most relevant threats and prevents tunnel vision.

runs.text: Applying all six STRIDE categories to every element is exhausting and produces many irrelevant results. STRIDE-per-element uses the DFD element type to focus the analysis. The standard matrix:

explanation.code:
Element Type     | S | T | R | I | D | E
-----------------|---|---|---|---|---|---
External entity  | X |   | X |   |   |
Process          | X | X | X | X | X | X
Data store       |   | X | ? | X | D |
Data flow        |   | X |   | X | X |

X = primary concern   D = DoS only (fill/delete)   ? = sometimes

runs.text: Reading the matrix in practice:

items.text: External entities
primarily face Spoofing (can the external actor fake their identity?) and Repudiation (can they deny their actions?).
Processes

are the most exposed — all six categories apply. A web application process can be spoofed (fake server cert), have its logic tampered with (code injection), repudiate actions (no logging), leak data, be DoS'd, or allow privilege escalation.
Data stores
face tampering (unauthorized writes), information disclosure (unauthorized reads), and a limited DoS (filling or deleting the store).
Data flows
face tampering (MITM modification), information disclosure (eavesdropping), and DoS (traffic flooding or dropping).

runs.text: The process is mechanical: for each element in the DFD, open the matrix, check which categories apply, and for each applicable category write one or more concrete threat statements. A threat statement names the attacker, the method, the element affected, and the impact.
Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (free, Windows) automates STRIDE-per-element generation from DFDs drawn in its editor. It is a practical starting point for teams new to the process.

STRIDE-per-element is a matrix that says: for each type of thing in your diagram, here are the threat categories most likely to apply. It focuses the analysis instead of asking you to check all six categories against everything.

cards.title: PASTA — Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis
cards.teaser: PASTA is a risk-centric, seven-stage threat modeling methodology that aligns security analysis with business objectives. Where STRIDE asks what could go wrong, PASTA asks what an attacker would actually do — and what it would cost the business.

runs.text: PASTA was introduced by Tony UcedaVélez and Marco Morana in
Risk Centric Threat Modeling
(2015). It is more heavyweight than STRIDE and is better suited to risk-driven organizations where threat modeling outputs must be justified in business terms.
The seven stages of PASTA:

items.text: Define business objectives.
What does the application protect? What are the compliance requirements? What is the business impact of a breach?
Define the technical scope.
Infrastructure inventory, network topology, technology stack. Establish the system boundary.
Decompose the application.
DFDs, use cases, trust levels, entry points. Same artifacts as DFD-based STRIDE, but framed around use cases.
Analyze threats.
Compile relevant threat intelligence: CVE databases, industry threat reports, attacker TTP (tactics, techniques, procedures) from MITRE ATT&CK.
Identify vulnerabilities.
Map known vulnerabilities (SAST, DAST, pen test findings) to the threats identified in stage 4.
Enumerate and model attacks.
Build attack trees for high-priority threats (see next card). Simulate attack paths.
Risk and impact analysis.
Score residual risk using CVSS or a qualitative model. Prioritize countermeasures. Produce a risk-ranked remediation backlog.

runs.text: PASTA's strength is traceability from business risk to technical control. Its weakness is time: a full PASTA engagement typically takes days. Use it for high-value systems (payment processing, PII stores) and use lighter methods for routine features.

PASTA works backwards from what a breach would cost the business, through what attackers would actually do, to which controls to implement. It produces a risk-ranked backlog rather than just a list of threats.

cards.title: Attack Trees
cards.teaser: Attack trees, introduced by Bruce Schneier in 1999, decompose an attacker's goal into a hierarchy of sub-goals. They make attack paths explicit, support AND/OR logic for path combinations, and can be annotated with cost and likelihood.

runs.text: Bruce Schneier published "Attack Trees" in
Dr. Dobb's Journal
(1999). The model is borrowed from fault trees in safety engineering. The root of the tree is the attacker's goal; branches represent sub-goals; leaves represent atomic attack steps.
Node types in an attack tree:

items.text: OR nodes
— any one child path is sufficient to achieve the parent goal. The parent is achieved if at least one branch succeeds.
AND nodes
— all child paths must be achieved. Models multi-step attacks where each step is a prerequisite.

runs.text: Example — attack tree for "Steal user credentials":

explanation.code:
GOAL: Steal user credentials (OR)
├── Phish the user (leaf)
├── Credential stuffing from leaked DB (leaf)
├── Intercept login (AND)
│   ├── Downgrade HTTPS to HTTP (leaf)
│   └── MITM the connection (leaf)
└── Compromise the auth service (AND)
    ├── Exploit a vulnerability (OR)
    │   ├── SQLi in login form (leaf)
    │   └── RCE via dependency CVE (leaf)
    └── Exfiltrate the credential store (leaf)

runs.text: Leaves can be annotated with attacker attributes: cost (how expensive is this step?), skill required (script kiddie vs nation state?), likelihood, and detectability. These attributes propagate up the tree using min/max operators, giving a composite score for each attack path.
Attack trees complement STRIDE: STRIDE identifies threat categories; attack trees model concrete multi-step attack paths for the highest-priority threats.

MITRE ATT&CK (attack.mitre.org) provides a knowledge base of real-world attacker TTPs that can be used to populate attack tree leaves with empirically observed techniques rather than hypothetical ones.

An attack tree starts with what the attacker wants at the top, then decomposes it into every way they could get there. AND branches mean they need all the steps; OR branches mean any one route will do.

cards.title: DREAD — Risk Rating for Individual Threats
cards.teaser: DREAD is a five-factor scoring model Microsoft used internally before CVSS became standard. Despite being largely superseded, it remains useful as a quick triage tool when CVSS scoring is overkill and informal 1–10 estimates are needed.

runs.text: DREAD was developed at Microsoft alongside STRIDE as a way to rank the threats STRIDE identified. Each threat is scored 1–10 on five factors; the scores are averaged (or summed) to produce a risk rating.

items.text: D — Damage potential.
How bad is a successful attack? Full system compromise = 10; minor data leak = 1.
R — Reproducibility.
How reliably can the attack be reproduced? Works every time = 10; requires specific rare conditions = 1.
E — Exploitability.
How easy is it to exploit? Public exploit kit available = 10; requires advanced custom tooling = 1.
A — Affected users.
What proportion of users are affected? All users = 10; single user = 1.
D — Discoverability.
How easily can an attacker find the vulnerability? Publicly documented = 10; requires internal access = 1.

runs.text: Microsoft discontinued DREAD internally around 2008, primarily because Discoverability created perverse incentives: security teams were tempted to suppress vulnerability documentation to lower the score rather than to fix the issue. CVSS removed discoverability from its base score for the same reason.
DREAD survives in practice for rapid whiteboard triage sessions where CVSS's 30+ parameters are too heavyweight and teams need a shared vocabulary to rank a list of threats in 30 minutes.

DREAD scores are subjective and non-reproducible across teams. Two analysts scoring the same threat can produce scores that differ by 3–4 points. Use it to establish rough priority ordering, not to make precise risk decisions.
DREAD scores a threat on five factors — how bad, how reliable, how easy to exploit, how many people affected, and how easy to find — then averages them into a risk number. Simple but subjective.

cards.title: CVSS — Common Vulnerability Scoring System
cards.teaser: CVSS is the industry standard for communicating the severity of vulnerabilities. A CVSS score is not a risk score — it quantifies the intrinsic properties of a vulnerability independent of the environment in which it appears.

runs.text: CVSS was developed by the National Infrastructure Advisory Council (NIAC) and is now maintained by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams). Version 3.1 is the current widely-deployed version; version 4.0 was released in 2023.
CVSS has three metric groups:

items.text: Base metrics

— the intrinsic properties of the vulnerability: Attack Vector (network/adjacent/local/physical), Attack Complexity, Privileges Required, User Interaction, Scope, and the CIA impact triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability). Base score range: 0.0–10.0.
Temporal metrics
— properties that change over time: exploit code maturity (is there a public exploit?), remediation level (is a patch available?), report confidence (how certain is the vulnerability report?).
Environmental metrics
— organization-specific adjustments: how important is the affected system to this specific business? A critical CVE in a library you do not use is effectively 0.

runs.text: Severity bands: Critical (9.0–10.0), High (7.0–8.9), Medium (4.0–6.9), Low (0.1–3.9), None (0.0). Most security teams triage Critical and High automatically; Medium is reviewed contextually.

The most important misunderstanding of CVSS: a 9.8 base score does not mean "your system is at critical risk." It means "this vulnerability type, if exploitable, would cause critical impact." The environmental score adjusts for your actual exposure. A 9.8 CVE in an internal library not reachable from the internet has much lower environmental priority.

NVD (nvd.nist.gov) publishes base CVSS scores for all CVEs. Vendors publish temporal scores when patches are available. Your security team should publish environmental scores for your specific deployment context.

CVSS scores how bad a vulnerability inherently is, not how risky it is for you specifically. The base score is universal; the environmental score adjusts it for your situation — a 10.0 CVE in software you do not run is not a priority.

cards.title: Risk Mitigation Strategies
cards.teaser: For every identified threat there are exactly four options: mitigate it, accept it, transfer it, or avoid it. Choosing deliberately is what turns a threat list into an engineering plan.

runs.text: The third question in Shostack's framework — "What are we going to do about it?" — has a finite answer space. Threat modeling teams should classify every threat into one of four categories before closing a session:

items.text: Mitigate

— implement a control that reduces the likelihood or impact of the threat. This is the most common response for high-severity threats. Examples: input validation, rate limiting, TLS, parameterized queries. Mitigation does not eliminate risk; it reduces it to a residual level.
Accept

— acknowledge the threat and consciously decide not to address it. Acceptable when the cost of mitigation exceeds the expected loss from the threat, or when the threat is sufficiently unlikely. Acceptance must be documented with a named owner and a review date — silent acceptance is negligence, not risk management.
Transfer

— shift financial or operational responsibility to another party. Cyber insurance transfers financial risk. Using a managed authentication provider (Auth0, AWS Cognito) transfers the operational risk of running an auth system. Transfer does not eliminate the threat — it changes who is responsible for the impact.
Avoid

— eliminate the feature or system element that introduces the threat. If storing credit card numbers introduces PCI scope, not storing them removes the threat entirely. Avoidance is underused: teams often mitigate threats they could simply avoid by redesigning the feature.

runs.text: All four responses should produce a backlog item (mitigate → engineering ticket; accept → risk register entry; transfer → vendor selection or insurance policy; avoid → product decision). A threat with no response is an unclosed risk.
"We'll address this later" is not risk acceptance — it is risk deferral with no commitment. Acceptance requires a named decision-maker, a documented rationale, and a review schedule.

Every threat you find needs one of four responses: fix it, own the risk consciously, pay someone else to handle it, or redesign to remove it entirely. Any threat without a response is just a note you never acted on.

cards.title: Threat-Model-as-Code
cards.teaser: Threat-model-as-code stores the DFD, trust boundaries, and threat assertions in version-controlled code, enabling diff reviews, CI enforcement, and automated threat generation. pytm is the leading open-source tool for this approach.

runs.text: Threat models stored only in Confluence pages or Miro boards have the same problem as undocumented architecture: they go stale the day after the meeting ends. Threat-model-as-code treats the threat model as a first-class engineering artifact that evolves with the codebase.
pytm (Python Threat Modeling) is the primary open-source DSL for this approach. A
pytm
model is a Python script that defines DFD elements programmatically:

explanation.code:
from pytm import TM, Server, Dataflow, Boundary, Actor, Datastore

tm = TM(name="Login Service", description="User authentication flow")

internet = Boundary(name="Internet")
internal = Boundary(name="Internal Network")

browser = Actor(name="User Browser", inBoundary=internet)
auth_svc = Server(name="Auth Service", inBoundary=internal, isHardened=True)
users_db = Datastore(name="Users DB", inBoundary=internal, isEncrypted=True)

login_req = Dataflow(
    browser, auth_svc, name="Login Request",
    protocol="HTTPS", isEncrypted=True
)
db_query = Dataflow(
    auth_svc, users_db, name="Credential Lookup",
    protocol="PostgreSQL"
)

tm.process()  # generates DFD diagram + STRIDE threat report

runs.text: Running
pytm

in CI produces a DFD image and a threat report. Pull request diffs show when trust boundaries change, when new data flows cross unprotected boundaries, or when security properties are removed. A CI gate can block merges that introduce unmitigated threats.

Other threat-modeling DSLs include OWASP Threat Dragon (visual, JSON-backed), IriusRisk (enterprise, GUI + API), and Foreseeti securiCAD (automated attack simulation). All share the principle that the model should live in source control and be reviewable like code.
pytm is maintained at github.com/izar/pytm. It generates DFDs via Graphviz and threat reports from a built-in STRIDE ruleset that can be extended with custom rules.

Threat-model-as-code means your DFD and threat list live in Git alongside the source code. When a developer adds a new data flow, the diff shows it, the CI pipeline checks it, and reviewers can see immediately whether a trust boundary was crossed without a control.

cards.title: Threat Modeling Cadence
cards.teaser: Threat modeling done once at project kickoff and never revisited is security theater. The model must be updated at design, at each major change, and after every significant incident — the system's threat surface evolves, and so must its model.

runs.text: One of the most common failure modes in threat modeling programs is the "big bang" model: a thorough threat model produced at the start of a project that is never touched again. By launch, the implementation has diverged from the model. Six months later, the model is a historical artifact.
A sustainable cadence has three trigger conditions:

items.text: At design time

— before writing code for a new feature or system. This is when the model is cheapest: the cost of a whiteboard change is zero; the cost of a shipped vulnerability is high. Even a 30-minute STRIDE walkthrough of a DFD sketch catches the most obvious issues.
At major change

— when significant architectural changes occur: new service integrations, new external data flows, new authentication mechanisms, changes to trust boundaries, or new data types (especially PII or payment data). A "major change" threshold should be defined explicitly in the team's engineering process.
Post-incident

— after a security incident or near-miss, update the threat model to include the attack path that was exploited or observed. This prevents the same attack from succeeding again and improves the model's fidelity to real-world threats.

runs.text: A lightweight continuous process: embed a 30-minute threat model review in the design review meeting for any feature that touches authentication, authorization, external data flows, or sensitive data. Reserve full-depth PASTA-style analysis for quarterly security reviews of high-value systems.

Shostack recommends treating the threat model as a living document in source control and scheduling a review checkpoint at each sprint that modifies a boundary or adds a new data flow. This makes threat modeling a normal part of the engineering process rather than a periodic audit.
Threat model once and you get a snapshot. Threat model at design, at major changes, and after incidents, and you get a living picture of your actual attack surface.

cards.title: STRIDE vs PASTA vs Attack Trees — Comparison
cards.teaser: STRIDE, PASTA, and attack trees are complementary, not competing. Understanding where each method excels prevents both under-engineering (STRIDE alone on a payment system) and over-engineering (full PASTA on a static marketing page).

runs.text: The three primary threat modeling methods differ in orientation, effort, and output. Choosing the right one (or combination) depends on team maturity, system criticality, and available time.

explanation.code:
Dimension        | STRIDE           | PASTA                | Attack Trees
-----------------|------------------|----------------------|--------------------
Orientation      | Defender-centric | Business risk-centric| Attacker-centric
Primary question | What could go    | What would it cost   | How would an
                 | wrong?           | if exploited?        | attacker get there?
Effort           | Low-Medium       | High                 | Medium
                 | (hours)          | (days)               | (hours per tree)
Output           | Categorized      | Risk-ranked          | Attack path
                 | threat list      | remediation backlog  | decomposition
Best for         | Early design     | High-value systems,  | Validating specific
                 | review, dev teams| compliance-driven    | high-priority threats
Tool support     | MS Threat        | IriusRisk,           | SeaSponge,
                 | Modeling Tool    | custom spreadsheets  | AttackTree+
Starts with      | DFD elements     | Business objectives  | Attacker goal
Quantification   | No (needs DREAD  | Yes (stage 7)        | Optional (leaf
                 | or CVSS)         |                      | annotations)

runs.text: In practice, the methods compose well:

items.text: Use STRIDE-per-element
to generate a comprehensive threat list from the DFD.
Use attack trees
to model the top 3–5 highest-priority threats from the STRIDE output in detail.
Use PASTA stages 4–7
to anchor the analysis in real-world threat intelligence and produce a business-justified remediation backlog.

runs.text: Shostack notes in his book that methodology choice matters less than doing threat modeling at all. A team that consistently runs 30-minute STRIDE sessions will have a more secure system than one that plans to run PASTA next quarter but never does.

STRIDE asks what categories of harm are possible; PASTA asks what the business impact is and builds a risk backlog; attack trees ask how specifically an attacker would execute a given goal. They work best used together.

cards.title: Putting It Together — A Threat Modeling Sprint
cards.teaser: A 90-minute threat modeling sprint using the four-questions framework, a DFD, and STRIDE-per-element produces more security value than a week of ad-hoc code review. The sprint structure makes threat modeling repeatable, not heroic.

runs.text: Most teams avoid threat modeling because it feels open-ended and expensive. A sprint structure fixes both problems. Here is a repeatable 90-minute format based on Shostack's four-questions framework:

items.text: Draw the DFD (20 minutes).
Whiteboard or digital. External entities, processes, data stores, flows, and trust boundaries. Every participant must agree the diagram is accurate before proceeding.
STRIDE-per-element pass (30 minutes).

Walk each DFD element. For each applicable STRIDE category, write one concrete threat statement: "An attacker could [action] against [element] by [method], causing [impact]." Time-box strictly — do not solve threats during this phase.
Triage and classify (20 minutes).
Apply DREAD or a simple High/Medium/Low rating to each threat. Classify each: mitigate, accept, transfer, or avoid. Assign an owner for every non-accepted item.
Retrospect (10 minutes).
Shostack's fourth question: Was the DFD accurate? Did we miss any major data flows? Were there threats we could not classify? Document gaps for the next session.
Output (10 minutes).

Commit the DFD to the repo (as pytm code or an image). File engineering tickets for mitigate items. Add accept items to the risk register. Assign transfer and avoid decisions to product/architecture owners.

runs.text: The session produces three artifacts: an updated DFD in source control, a risk-classified threat list, and a set of actionable backlog items. All three can be reviewed in the next sprint retrospective to answer Shostack's fourth question: "Did we do a good job?"

Security engineers are not required for a threat modeling sprint. With training, feature engineers and architects can run the STRIDE pass themselves. The security team's role is to set the process, review outputs, and escalate complex threats — not to be the bottleneck on every session.

A 90-minute threat modeling sprint has five steps: draw the diagram, brainstorm threats by category, rank and classify each threat, check your own work, then commit the outputs. Repeatable process beats occasional heroics.
